notes.title: Field Notes, Vol. I — On the Topology of Attention
notes.excerpt: A loose collection of observations gathered at the edge of focus and distraction — what the landscape looks like when the mind finally stops moving.
notes.summary: A field observation cross-referencing Simone Weil's writings on attention with modern cognitive science. The territory between focus and distraction turns out to be inhabited. Conclusions provisional but pointing somewhere interesting.

notes.title: A Working Theory of Adjacent Possible
notes.excerpt: Stuart Kauffman's phrase keeps appearing on different maps. I suspect it describes something important about how interesting problems self-select their solvers.
notes.summary: An attempt to map how Kauffman's adjacent possible functions as a predictive tool for intellectual adjacency. The model wants refinement. Still being cross-referenced against the primary literature.

notes.title: Marginalia: Tools That Think With You
notes.excerpt: Notes toward a typology of tools that extend cognition rather than merely automate it. The distinction matters more than most product teams admit.
notes.summary: Toward a typology of cognitive-extension tools versus automation tools. The distinction carries real design implications — implications most teams have not yet reckoned with. More specimen examples needed before the taxonomy holds.

notes.title: On Reading Maps That Lie
notes.excerpt: Every map is an argument. Some arguments are honest about their limitations; most are not. A meditation on epistemics, cartography, and institutional knowledge.
notes.summary: Every map is an argument — this dispatch traces what it means when the argument is dishonest by design. Draws from cartographic history and the politics of institutional knowledge-making. Still unresolved at its core.

notes.title: The Shape of a Good Question
notes.excerpt: Most questions are really conclusions in disguise. The ones worth holding open for years have a particular shape — pointed enough to aim at something, loose enough to surprise you.
notes.summary: A taxonomy of question-shapes and what makes certain questions worth holding open for years. Still resolving the line between productive ambiguity and productive specificity. The shape is becoming clearer.

notes.title: Notes on Legibility and Scale
notes.excerpt: What it means for a system to remain understandable as it grows — and why most systems fail at this not through malice but through accumulation.
notes.summary: What it means for a system to remain understandable under growth pressure. Most legibility failures are failures of accumulation, not design intent. Patterns are emerging but not yet codified into a usable model.
